overview.summary: Import distributors source goods offshore, manage freight, Customs and product compliance, hold inventory and sell through business, retail, dealer or direct channels. New Zealand's distance from suppliers and relatively small market can require long lead times and meaningful safety stock. Economic value comes from supplier rights, product knowledge, local inventory availability, channel access and after-sales support, while credit risk centres on foreign exchange, landed cost, stock quality, concentration and working-capital funding.
business_models: Exclusive or authorised distribution of overseas brands
Non-exclusive wholesale of consumer, trade or industrial products
Private-label importing with local brand ownership
Industrial distribution combining stock, technical sales, installation, parts and service
Direct-to-consumer import retail alongside dealer or wholesale channels
industry_structure: Global suppliers, local distributors, wholesalers, retailers and direct e-commerce can compete in the same product chain.
Local scale, stock availability, technical support and established channels can offset limited purchasing volume.
Supplier and customer concentration are common, and exclusivity may be territory-, performance- or change-of-control dependent.
demand_drivers: Domestic consumption, construction, agriculture, manufacturing and maintenance
Product replacement, installed base and after-sales parts
Price, exchange rates, brand, availability, service and channel coverage
Population, business investment and product regulation
margin_and_cost_drivers: Supplier pricing, foreign exchange, freight, duty, GST, port and storage cost
Sales mix, rebates, exclusivity, channel discounts and price pass-through
Inventory turns, obsolescence, damage, warranty and returns
Warehouse, sales, technical support and last-mile fulfilment
cyclicality_and_seasonality: Exposure follows end markets and may include consumer, construction or capital-equipment cycles.
Shipping schedules, supplier shutdowns, peak retail periods and agricultural seasons can concentrate stock purchases.
Currency and freight shocks may move landed cost faster than local prices.
overview.working_capital_profile: The model is commonly working-capital intensive. Deposits or supplier payment, sea transit, Customs clearance and warehousing occur before customer collection, and long lead times encourage safety stock. Growth can therefore increase profit and borrowing simultaneously. Inventory must be assessed by SKU, age, demand, ownership, location and net realisable value, while landed-cost accounting and foreign-currency payables require reconciliation.
overview.asset_intensity: Physical fixed assets may be moderate, but inventory, warehouse systems, racking, vehicles, technical equipment and working capital are central. Stock can support a borrowing base only after eligibility and concentration reserves. Supplier rights, local brand, channel relationships and product expertise can be valuable but are not reliable standalone collateral.
regulatory_and_compliance: Customs import entries, valuation, tariff, duty, GST, prohibited and restricted goods
Biosecurity, food, hazardous substance, electrical, building or other product approvals
Fair Trading, Consumer Guarantees, product safety, labelling, warranty and recalls
Health and safety duties applying to importers and suppliers of workplace plant or substances

subsectors.name: Consumer-goods import distribution
subsectors.business_model: Branded or private-label products are imported and supplied to retailers, dealers or consumers.
subsectors.working_capital: Seasonal buys, retailer terms and SKU breadth create stock and receivable funding needs.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Inventory and brand-building are more important than plant.

subsectors.name: Industrial and technical distribution
subsectors.business_model: Equipment, components, consumables or parts are sold with technical advice, installation and service.
subsectors.working_capital: Slow-moving critical parts may be strategically necessary despite low turns; capital equipment can be high value.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Inventory, demonstration units, service equipment and technical systems.

subsectors.name: Food and beverage importing
subsectors.business_model: Food or beverage products are imported under registered, traceable supply arrangements and sold wholesale or retail.
subsectors.working_capital: Shelf life, temperature, batch traceability and seasonal inventory determine recovery.
subsectors.asset_intensity: Inventory and temperature-controlled storage may be significant.

subsectors.name: Building and trade-product distribution
subsectors.business_model: Products are imported and sold to merchants, contractors, fabricators or projects.
subsectors.working_capital: Bulk buys and project orders create stock peaks; certification changes can impair inventory.

primary_risks.risk: Foreign exchange, freight and landed-cost volatility
primary_risks.mechanism: Supplier currency and freight move before local prices reset, compressing gross margin and increasing funding.
Long lead times create high safety stock and exposure to obsolescence, expiry, specification change or demand error.
Loss of an overseas supplier, exclusive right, major retailer or dealer channel can impair sales and leave stock stranded.
financial_signals: Gross profit by supplier and customer

primary_risks.mechanism: Customs, biosecurity, safety or product failure can delay clearance, stop sales and create remediation cost.

cash_conversion_and_working_capital: Build the cash cycle from supplier deposit through transit, clearance, stock holding, sale and customer collection.
Reconcile inventory to SKU-level aging, title, location, demand and net realisable value.
Separate trade creditors, foreign-currency payables, Customs and GST, customer deposits and stock finance.
Stress growth, supplier-term tightening, exchange rates and slower stock turns together.
collateral_considerations: Inventory borrowing bases require eligible categories, aging, concentration, title and realisable-value reserves.
Stock in transit, consigned goods, food near expiry, unsupported products and customer-specific items need conservative treatment.
Receivables should be adjusted for rebates, returns, warranties, disputes and customer concentration.
Supplier retention, Customs claims, floorplan financiers and other security interests can affect priority.
downside_stresses: Currency depreciation and freight increase with delayed repricing
Loss of a major supplier or customer
Slower stock turns plus inventory write-down
monitoring_kpis: Sales and gross profit by supplier, product and customer
Landed margin and FX hedge position
Inventory days, aging, sell-through and write-downs
Liquidity, borrowing-base headroom, leverage and DSCR
covenant_considerations: Borrowing-base reporting with stock and debtor eligibility
Notice of supplier termination, recall, clearance issue or material inventory write-down
diligence_questions: What is the complete landed cost and how quickly can exchange rate or freight changes be repriced?
Which stock is aged, slow, seasonal, expiring, consigned, in transit or tied to one customer or standard?
Are supplier and exclusivity agreements current, transferable and subject to minimum purchases?
Which Customs, MPI, safety, labelling and product certifications apply?
What security interests, supplier title or stock-finance claims rank against inventory and receivables?

value_drivers: Durable transferable supplier rights and owned brands
Strong stock turns and landed-margin control
Installed base, technical support and recurring aftermarket
Effective sourcing, compliance and management systems
multiple_influences: Exclusive distribution and recurring aftermarket can improve predictability where agreements transfer.
Headline revenue is less meaningful without comparable gross margin and working-capital intensity.
Supplier concentration, aged stock, currency exposure and minimum-purchase commitments reduce value.
normalisation_focus: Normal FX, freight and landed margin
Inventory write-downs and warranty or recall cost
Market owner sales and product-management remuneration
Supplier rebates and one-off stock gains
Sustainable working capital and warehouse cost
peer_selection: Match consumer versus industrial, wholesale versus direct, exclusive versus non-exclusive and product end market.
Compare gross margin, stock turns, customer and supplier concentration, working capital and aftermarket.
Separate owned-brand economics from agency-only distribution.
preferred_metrics: EV/gross profit for carefully aligned distributor economics
EV/revenue only where gross margin and mix are genuinely comparable
DCF or free cash flow after inventory investment
discount_and_premium_factors: Premium indicators include transferable exclusivity, owned brand, diverse channels, strong turns and recurring parts or consumables.
Discount indicators include supplier termination risk, obsolete stock, thin margin, FX exposure and key-person product relationships.
diligence_questions: Will supplier, brand and customer arrangements transfer on completion?
What inventory and working capital must remain for normal service?
What is maintainable margin after currency, freight, rebates, warranty and obsolescence?
How dependent are sourcing, pricing and channel relationships on the owner?

market_research_sections.credit_paper:
Import distribution is an important link in New Zealand's trade-dependent supply chain. Customs requires commercial goods to be cleared and appropriate entries, duties, GST and restricted-goods documentation to be addressed, while Stats NZ merchandise-trade and wholesale data provide market context. These aggregate sources do not prove the borrower's demand or stock quality. Credit analysis should map the entire cash cycle from foreign supplier deposit and transit through clearance, warehousing, sale and customer collection.

Foreign exchange, freight and supplier-price changes can increase landed cost before customer pricing resets. Long lead times and a small market often require safety stock, so growth may consume borrowing headroom. Inventory must be assessed by SKU, age, title, location, demand, expiry or specification and net realisable value; stock in transit, consigned, unsupported or customer-specific goods deserve additional reserves. Customer receivables should be adjusted for rebates, returns, warranty and concentration.

Supplier and exclusivity terms, minimum purchases, change of control, channel concentration and product compliance can determine continuity. Food, plant, electrical, building or hazardous products may have additional MPI, WorkSafe or product-safety duties. The credit paper should stress currency and freight, slower turns, supplier or customer loss and recall, then set security and monitoring around an evidence-based borrowing base rather than book inventory.
market_research_sections.valuation_report:
An import distributor creates value by combining supplier access, product and regulatory knowledge, local stock availability, channel relationships, brand and after-sales support. Stats NZ trade and wholesale series can frame import and sector activity, but maintainable value depends on the subject's landed margin, supplier and customer concentration, stock turns, agreement transferability and working-capital intensity. Consumer, industrial, food and building-product distributors require different peers.

Normalised earnings should reflect representative foreign exchange and freight, rebates, warranty, obsolescence, owner sales and product-management remuneration and the warehouse and working capital needed to support service. Inventory should be reviewed at completion because book cost may include slow, expired, unsupported or customer-specific items. An exclusive agreement is not automatically valuable if it is short, non-transferable, subject to onerous minimum purchases or easily replaced by direct supply.

Transferable value is stronger where supplier rights are durable, brands or data are owned, customers and channels are diverse, stock turns are controlled and the business has recurring parts, consumables or service income. Key-supplier dependence, thin margins, currency exposure, aged stock, recall risk and owner-held sourcing relationships reduce forecast confidence. This pack supports diligence and peer selection; it does not provide a current distributor multiple or inventory appraisal.

limitations: Import economics vary by product, supplier country, regulation, channel and foreign currency.
Supplier agreements, stock aging, title, compliance and customer demand require subject-specific evidence.
Trade, exchange-rate, freight and regulatory conditions are time-sensitive and should be refreshed at the report date.
No current valuation multiple, currency forecast, borrowing-base advance rate or inventory recovery value is supplied.
